title: Join algorithms
lead: Nested-loop, indexed, sort-merge and hash joins with explicit page-I/O assumptions.

sections.title: Nested-loop joins
sections.html:
Let R have M pages and m tuples, S have N pages, and let B be the number of buffer frames. The source counts input and temporary-page I/O, ignoring CPU and final output writes equally across algorithms.

Tuple nested loops scans S for every tuple in R: M + mN. Page nested loops scans S for each page of R: M + MN. Block nested loops uses B − 2 frames for an outer block, one for inner input and one for output: M + ⌈M/(B − 2)⌉N.

Compute both orientations because changing outer and inner changes the cost. When the outer input fits in B − 2 frames, block nested loops reads each input once, costing M + N.

PDF pp. 1–11

sections.title: Index nested-loop join
sections.html:
Index nested loops scans the outer relation and probes an index on the inner join attribute for each outer tuple. Its cost is M + m·lookupCost, where lookupCost includes both index navigation and fetching all matching inner records.

A clustered index groups matching records on relatively few data pages. An unclustered index can cause many random data-page fetches. A hash index supports equality; an appropriate tree index can support ordered comparisons.

The number of matches per outer key matters. A cheap index lookup does not imply a cheap join if each probe returns many records. Existing order, buffer reuse and whether the index already exists also affect the comparison.

PDF pp. 12–15

sections.title: Sort-merge join
sections.html:
Sort-merge join sorts both inputs on the join key, then advances through them in key order. When keys match, it emits all matching pairs. Duplicate groups require the cross-product of the two groups, not a single output pair.

The usual merge read cost is M + N when duplicate groups can be processed without repeated disk scans. Total cost adds sorting both inputs. Large duplicate groups can require rereading or spilling; the source notes a nested-loop-like worst case.

The slide example with M = 1000, N = 500 and B = 100 costs 4000 + 2000 + 1500 = 7500 I/Os with separate sorting and merging. If the last sort passes are fused with the join and the input runs fit the buffer budget, the cost becomes 4500.

PDF pp. 16–33

sections.title: Hash join and algorithm choice
sections.html:
An in-memory hash join builds a hash table on one input and probes it with the other. Matching hash values still require key comparison. It supports equijoins and must output every matching tuple combination.

Grace hash join partitions both inputs using the same join-key hash function. It then builds and probes each corresponding partition pair. One partitioning level costs 3(M + N): read/write both inputs, then read them for joining. The build partition’s hash table must fit memory; otherwise recursive partitioning or another strategy is needed.

Hashing benefits from a small build input; sorting benefits from existing or required order. Nested loops permits general predicates, and indexed nested loops benefits from selective probes. Costs must be compared with consistent memory and output assumptions.

PDF pp. 34–43

quiz.question: Two groups with the same key contain 3 and 4 tuples. How many joined tuples do they produce?
quiz.explanation: Pair each of the three first-input occurrences with all four second-input occurrences: 4+4+4=12 output tuples. A join does not deduplicate the groups. Sorting or hashing can organise the comparisons differently, but cannot discard any of these valid pairs.
